question: A patient is brought to the emergency department unresponsive with a respiratory rate of 4/min and bilateral pinpoint pupils. What is the immediate pharmacological treatment?

answers.text: IV naloxone 0.4–2 mg — competitive antagonist at opioid receptors that reverses respiratory depression and coma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The triad of coma + miosis (pinpoint pupils) + respiratory depression is pathognomonic for opioid overdose. Naloxone competitively displaces opioids from µ, κ, and δ receptors, rapidly reversing respiratory depression (onset 1–2 min IV). Its short half-life (30–90 min) means re-narcotisation can occur with long-acting opioids — repeat dosing or infusion may be needed.

answers.text: IV flumazenil — reverses all forms of CNS depression including opioid sedation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Flumazenil is specific for benzodiazepine reversal (GABA-A BZD-site antagonist). It has no activity at opioid receptors. BZD overdose causes coma and respiratory depression but does NOT cause miosis — pupil size is normal or slightly dilated.

answers.text: IV dextrose 50% — hypoglycaemia is the most common cause of pinpoint pupils with coma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hypoglycaemia causes coma but does NOT cause miosis. Blood glucose should always be checked (it is a reversible cause of coma), but pinpoint pupils point specifically to opioid toxicity or pontine haemorrhage. The clinical context (syringe, track marks, respiratory depression) confirms opioid overdose.

answers.text: IV physostigmine — reverses the anticholinergic crisis causing miosis and respiratory depression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anticholinergic toxicity causes mydriasis (dilated pupils), not miosis. Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity (tachycardia, dry skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention). Pinpoint pupils indicate cholinergic excess or opioid toxicity — the opposite of anticholinergic.

overallFeedback.feedback: Always match the antidote to the toxidrome: opioid overdose (coma, miosis, bradypnoea) → naloxone; BZD overdose (coma, normal pupils) → flumazenil; anticholinergic toxicity (mydriasis, tachycardia, dry) → physostigmine.

The opioid overdose triad (coma + miosis + respiratory depression) demands immediate naloxone. Remember: naloxone's half-life is shorter than most opioids — monitor for re-narcotisation and be prepared to repeat doses.
